title: Floor and Box Puzzles: Vertical Arrangements Made Routine

questions.question: In a 5-floor puzzle (bottom = floor 1), Q lives on an odd-numbered floor below 4, R immediately above Q, T on the top floor, P immediately below S, and P on the bottom floor. On which floor does Q live?
questions.rationale: T = 5 (top floor). P = 1 (bottom), so S = 2 sits immediately above P. The remaining floors 3 and 4 take the Q/R pair: Q must be odd and below 4, so Q = 3 with R = 4 immediately above. Final: P1, S2, Q3, R4, T5 — one anchor per clue, no trial and error.

questions.question: Six boxes A-F are stacked (position 1 = bottom). A is immediately above C; C is second from the bottom; E is at the top; D is immediately below B; B is below A. Which box is at the bottom?
questions.rationale: C = 2, so A = 3; E = 6. The B/D pair with B above D must fit below A among slots 1 and 4/5: only (D4, B5) works, leaving F = 1. Bottom to top: F, C, A, D, B, E.

questions.question: In floor puzzles, the conventional numbering unless stated otherwise is:
questions.rationale: The standard convention numbers the ground/lowest floor 1 and rises from there. The first move in every puzzle is to write the numbers on your diagram — and to re-check the wording when a question says 'the top floor is numbered 1' instead.

questions.question: The clue 'there are two boxes between A and B' means the positions of A and B differ by:
questions.rationale: Two boxes BETWEEN means two intervening positions, so the gap in position numbers is 3. Confusing position-gap with box-count (answering 2) is the topic's most common trap.

questions.question: In a two-flat-per-floor arrangement, 'B lives immediately above A in the same flat' means:
options: B is one floor up, same flat number
B is one flat across, same floor
B is one floor up, any flat
B and A are on the same floor
questions.rationale: 'Same flat' copies the column; 'immediately above' shifts the row by +1. Two-dimensional clues always decompose into a row instruction and a column instruction — draw the grid.

questions.question: Which clue type should you place FIRST when solving a floor puzzle?
questions.rationale: Definite clues ('G lives on floor 3') fix anchors outright, shrinking every later choice. Relative clues need an anchor to attach to, and negative clues only prune — they come last, to break ties.

questions.question: In an 8-floor building, T lives on floor 6 and R's floor is three away from T's. Where does R live?
questions.rationale: Candidates are 6 + 3 = 9 and 6 - 3 = 3. Floor 9 does not exist in an 8-floor building, so the stack's own limits force R = 3 — direction-finding from building size, no trial and error.

questions.question: 'As many floors above X as below Y' on floors 1-9 with X on floor 3 puts Y on:
questions.rationale: Floors above X: 9 - 3 = 6. Floors below Y must also be 6, so Y - 1 = 6 and Y = 7. The trap is forgetting that 'below floor Y' counts Y - 1 floors, not Y.

questions.question: When a floor puzzle's clues seem to produce TWO complete valid arrangements, the correct response is:
options: Re-read the clues for a missed discriminator (especially negatives)
questions.rationale: Well-formed exam puzzles have exactly one solution — a surviving second arrangement means a clue (usually a negative one) was skipped or an either/or was collapsed prematurely. Audit unused clues before matching options.

questions.question: Floor puzzles and box-stack puzzles are best treated as:
options: The same skeleton with different furniture
questions.rationale: Both are numbered vertical stacks processed by definite-then-relative-then-negative clues, with identical arithmetic (+1 for immediately above, position gaps for between-counts). Shelves and berths join the same family — one method covers all.
